facts.text: Studio execs only wanted Stan Winston's shop to build the monster. Winston said he'd do the creature only if he could direct, so this became his directing debut.
Star Lance Henriksen had dentures made for a rural look and brought his own props: a WWII pump shotgun, his cap, and the silver dollars he hands the witch.
Co-writer Gary Gerani says Ed Justin's poem had nothing to do with revenge or a demon. The writers' own 1970s demon-of-revenge idea was merged with the title and rhyme.
Mushroom, the dog who plays the dog here, did his own stunts. Four years earlier he played Billy's dog Barney in Gremlins (1984).
The teens' cabin is the same house used as the Jarvis house in Friday the 13th: The Final Chapter. It's at Kelly Gulch in Topanga, California.
Pumpkinhead was the film debut of Mayim Bialik, who plays Christine Wallace, one of the backwoods Wallace kids.
An opening diner scene introducing the city teens was filmed, then cut by Stan Winston. Co-writer Gary Gerani later said Winston was right to cut it.
Lance Henriksen collected the silver dollars himself from pawn shops. Most fell through the floorboards of the witch's shack, where he says they may still lie.
Florence Schauffler's witch costume weighed about 65 pounds. In makeup she stayed in character between takes and would only answer to the name Haggis.
Makeup artist Shane Mahan made nine sets of witch appliances and gave her an oversized ceramic eye lens, an idea borrowed from Christopher Lee's Frankenstein monster.
Made for about $3.5 million, Pumpkinhead grossed only $4,385,516 in US theaters. Cult status came later, mostly via home video.
To save wear on the suit, performer Tom Woodruff Jr. was glued into the Pumpkinhead costume at the start of the day and stayed inside for up to eight hours.
Lance Henriksen almost passed over the odd title, but one scene, the dead son speaking to Ed Harley, sold him: "It made me do the movie, that one scene."
Production designer Cynthia Charette said the run-down hill-folk shanties were inspired by the paintings and installations of artist Robert Rauschenberg.
The producer, De Laurentiis Entertainment Group, went bankrupt. United Artists picked up the film and tested it under the title Vengeance - The Demon.
Co-writer Gary Gerani says the demon's Lovecraftian look traces back to a hooded Don Post Creature from the Black Lagoon mask the writers used as a stand-in for their idea.
Screenwriters Mark Patrick Carducci and Gary Gerani drew inspiration from the horror films of Italian director Mario Bava.
Shane Mahan gave the witch no fake teeth, only color. He didn't want hissing or slurring in her key explanation scene: "If that's not convincing, the rest of the movie just doesn't work."
Co-writer Mark Patrick Carducci also wrote Neon Maniacs. He died in 1997 at age 42.
Star Lance Henriksen's character name, Ed Harley, is also an alias Chevy Chase uses in Fletch Lives (1989), where he claims to be Ed Harley of Harley-Davidson.
Two of director Stan Winston's own children can be glimpsed among the backwoods Wallace clan.
Effects artist Shane Mahan says filmmakers still cite Pumpkinhead as a model for making an effective low-budget movie, all done in-camera for about $3 million.
Horror punk band The Misfits wrote a song called "Pumpkin Head" for their 1999 album Famous Monsters.
The film's production company, De Laurentiis Entertainment Group, also made Blue Velvet and Evil Dead II before going bankrupt two years after its 1986 start.
Buck Flower, who plays Mr. Wallace, is a prolific character actor usually cast as a drunk or a bum. He called working for Stan Winston a pleasant experience.
Effects artist Alec Gillis recalled director Stan Winston cocking his glasses at a weird angle across a tense cabin set just to make him laugh.
James Cameron originally pictured Lance Henriksen as the title killer in The Terminator, even drawing concept art. Henriksen ended up as a cop, then Bishop in Aliens, where he met Stan Winston.
Reviews were mixed: Chicago Tribune critic Dave Kehr wrote Stan Winston "knows how to make a monster" but not how to bring one to life. Rotten Tomatoes sits at 51%.
Critic John Kenneth Muir called Pumpkinhead "a meditation on vengeance" in Horror Films of the 1980s, praising it for rejecting the decade's popular vigilante-justice theme.
Electronic Arts released a PC first-person shooter, Bloodwings: Pumpkinhead's Revenge, in 1995. It was poorly received.
Jeff East, who plays Chris, played teen Clark Kent in Superman: The Movie (1978) and Huckleberry Finn in 1974's Huckleberry Finn.
A 1993 Dark Horse Pumpkinhead comic planned four issues but only two were published. The second ended on a cliffhanger promising a winged Pumpkinhead.
As the demon's victims pile up, its face grows more human and resembles Ed Harley's, since Lance Henriksen's features were the basis for the creature design.
Lance Henriksen returned as Ed Harley in two 2006-07 Syfy sequels but has called them terrible, while staying proud of the original.
A Pumpkinhead reboot was reported in development at Paramount Players in 2021, with a script ready. No director has been announced.
Co-writer Gary Gerani and producer Billy Blake once pitched a reboot that would have cast Josh Brolin as Ed Harley. Gerani says it went nowhere.
While shooting Predator, Stan Winston found frogs in his hotel shower and blamed Arnold Schwarzenegger. His crew had actually done it, and let him get revenge on Arnold anyway.
Pumpkinhead has fans including novelist Anne Rice and many Stan Winston Studio crew members who worked on it.
